title: Keep the secret out
briefing: The ~/api project has source files — and a .env file holding a database
password. That secret must NEVER go into git; committed secrets are one of
the most common ways credentials leak.
Put ~/api under version control, but make git ignore .env so it's never
tips: A .gitignore file, one pattern per line, tells git what to skip. Create it BEFORE you `git add .`.
Check with `git status`: once .env is ignored, it stops appearing as untracked.
objective: Make ~/api a git repo and commit its files, but keep .env out of git by ignoring it — .env must not be tracked.
expert_objective: Version ~/api without ever tracking its .env secret.
hints: Start the repo and tell git to ignore the secret: `cd ~/api && git init`, then `echo .env > .gitignore`.
Now stage and commit everything else: `git add .` (the ignored .env is skipped), then `git commit -m "initial commit"`.
`cd ~/api && git init && echo .env > .gitignore && git add . && git commit -m "init"`. `git status` shows .env is no longer listed.
solution:
cd ~/api
git init
echo .env > .gitignore
git add .
git commit -m "initial commit"
explanation: `.gitignore` lists paths git should pretend it can't see — secrets, build output, logs. Add the pattern before you stage, and `git add .` quietly skips it. That's how you keep a .env of passwords out of a repo that might one day be pushed somewhere public.
